content: Cardiotocography (CTG) is a medical technique used in obstetrics to monitor and record the fetal heartbeat and uterine contractions during childbirth. The term cardiotocography is derived from cardioreferring to the fetal heart and -toco referring to uterine contractions, with -graphy indicating the recording process. This method is particularly useful for identifying signs of fetal distress. The recordings in CTG are obtained using two separate transducers. One transducer is responsible for measuring the fetal pulse, while the other measures uterine contractions. In external monitoring, these transducers are attached to the abdominal wall using straps or adhesive electrodes. The heart electrode is positioned over the area corresponding to the fetal heart, while the contraction electrode measures the tension of the abdominal wall, which serves as an indirect indicator of intrauterine pressure. Internal monitoring, on the other hand, requires a certain degree of cervical dilation. This method involves inserting a pressure catheter into the uterine cavity to measure intrauterine pressure directly. Additionally, a scalp electrode is attached to the fetus's head to obtain a more accurate measurement of the fetal heart rate. Internal monitoring is generally more precise and is often preferred in cases where a complicated childbirth is anticipated. The data collected during CTG is typically printed on paper or stored digitally on a computer for future reference. The interpretation of CTG involves analyzing the timing of uterine contractions in relation to the variability of the fetal heart rate (FHR). Abnormalities in the baseline fetal heart rate, such as bradycardia (slower than normal heart rate) or tachycardia (faster than normal heart rate), are evaluated in the context of the clinical presentation. A lack of variability in the FHR may also be significant. Decelerations, or temporary slowing of the fetal heart rate, are categorized based on their timing relative to uterine contractions. Type I decelerations, which occur during a contraction and resolve as the contraction ends, are considered normal. However, Type II decelerations, characterized by a further slowing of the fetal heart rate after the contraction has resolved, are generally regarded as pathological. These late decelerations are often interpreted as a sign of fetal distress and may warrant further clinical intervention.
